# National income accounts (GDP) (`national_accounts_gdp`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/economy.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Economy & finance (`economy`)
- Deps: helped by double_entry, census_vital_registration, economic_growth_productivity
- Core idea: Measure production inside the territory. Add producers’ output minus intermediate inputs, then add taxes less subsidies on products to obtain GDP at market prices. Equivalently add household consumption, investment, government consumption and exports less imports. The income measure includes operating surplus as well as wages and taxes less subsidies on production and imports. Adjust for price changes to compare real output over time. GDP measures a flow of production, distinct from the stock of wealth or the revenue a government can collect. Counting value added avoids counting the wheat in the bread twice.
- Pitfalls:
  - Double counting intermediate goods (wheat, flour and bread all added at full value)
  - Comparing money totals across years without removing inflation
  - Treating GDP as welfare: it ignores leisure, health, unpaid household work and depletion of resources
  - Leaving out subsistence farming, which in pre-industrial economies is most of output
- History: europe: 1665 – William Petty's Verbum Sapienti estimates England's income; 1696 Gregory King's table for 1688; 1941 Meade and Stone's national income white paper for Britain; americas: 1934 – Kuznets' national income estimates for the US Senate; 1942 wartime gross national product estimates; global: 1953 – UN System of National Accounts
- Read:
  - Simon Kuznets, National Income, 1929–1932 (1934)
  - Diane Coyle, GDP: A Brief but Affectionate History (2014)
